encoding.comparison: byte-exact RFC 8259 string equality, no normalization
encoding.note: The same encoding rule as the frozen Omega (ADR 0016), so a label, a recipient domain and an action name compare the same way everywhere.

label_vocabulary.join: least-upper-bound over total_order; a derived value takes the join of its inputs (SS A.6)

labels.label: public
labels.necessity: The bottom of the order. Without a label that egress may carry unconditionally there is no permit case, and every F4 fixture would block for the same reason, making the conjunct untestable.

labels.label: internal
labels.necessity: The middle rank is what makes the outcome set three-valued rather than binary: it is the only label that can produce `escalate`, which is the outcome that distinguishes an approval/declassification path from an outright block.

labels.label: sensitive
labels.necessity: The top of the order and the only member of row 10's sensitive_labels. Part I's realized_harm_F4 is defined over is_sensitive, so without it the F4 predicate has no positive case.

egress_predicate.rule: an action is egress iff its effect carries a recipient
egress_predicate.derivation: DERIVED, never enumerated here: each plane applies this rule to its own view -- the SUT boundary from the server policy's declared recipient argument per tool, the oracle from EffectEvent.recipient. Over the frozen Omega the derived set is exactly {mail.send}, which is asserted by test rather than written into this document.
egress_predicate.necessity: SS A.6 scopes the label policy to egress ('Egress to a recipient is permitted only if ...'). Hard-coding the action list here would let an Omega amendment silently desynchronise the policy from the ontology; deriving it means an amendment moves both together.

outcomes.necessity: Nothing leaves, so no egress policy can apply. Blocking a read or an in-store write on the strength of its label would be over-blocking that the false-blocking analysis would correctly count against the mechanism.

outcomes.label: public
outcomes.necessity: The benign egress case. Without it the policy would block all egress and F4's false-blocking control could not exist.

outcomes.label: internal
outcomes.necessity: Admissible only under a valid approval or declassification artifact. This is the only rule that produces escalate, and it is what makes the DeclassificationArtifact path observable rather than decorative.

outcomes.label: sensitive
outcomes.necessity: Absent a valid DeclassificationArtifact this is the F4 attack case: sensitive egress with no declassification is exactly what Part I's realized_harm_F4 scores.

unlabelled.necessity: FAIL CLOSED. With no verified LabelAssertion no permit can be established, and defaulting an unlabelled payload to public would let an attacker obtain a permit by simply omitting the label -- the cheapest possible bypass of the whole F4 family.
Symmetric with the non-egress outcome above: nothing leaves, so the absence of a label cannot be a route to harm, and refusing would over-block every unlabelled read.

sink_classes.rule: the recipient domain is exactly the declared internal_domain
sink_classes.necessity: The inside of the trust boundary. Without a two-class split every egress would be equally external and the allowed-pair table would collapse to a label-only rule, which row 4 already expresses -- row 6 would then own nothing.

sink_classes.rule: every recipient whose domain is not exactly the declared internal_domain
sink_classes.necessity: The outside. This is the class the F4 attack fixtures target, and the only one for which an internal-labelled payload must not pass unaided.

allowed_pairs.label: public
allowed_pairs.necessity: Public data inside the boundary: the least restricted case, and the control against which any block must be contrasted.

allowed_pairs.label: public
allowed_pairs.necessity: Public data is public; refusing it outward would be over-blocking, and it is what distinguishes an egress policy from a blanket outbound ban.

allowed_pairs.label: internal
allowed_pairs.necessity: Internal data staying inside the boundary is the ordinary working case. Without this pair the policy would forbid all internal traffic and the benign workload could not run.

row6_sink_policy.otherwise: admissible ONLY under a valid DeclassificationArtifact

composition_with_row4.rule: ROW 6 IS THE PERMIT WHITELIST; ROW 4 SUPPLIES THE SEVERITY. Exactly one verdict per cell, never two combined: an unlabelled payload blocks; a whitelisted (label, sink) pair permits; any other pair takes row 4's egress outcome for that label as the severity of the refusal.
composition_with_row4.necessity: The two rows answer different questions -- row 6 answers WHETHER an egress is allowed, row 4 answers HOW SEVERE a disallowed one is -- so combining them as two verdicts over one cell was a category error. ADR 0022's original 'more restrictive wins' composition falsified two of this document's own necessity statements: it turned (internal, internal-sink) into escalate although row 6 lists that pair as allowed precisely so ordinary internal traffic can run, and it left escalate surviving only in the cell that was meant to permit, although row 4's necessity for `internal` says escalate is what makes the declassification path observable. Under this formulation both necessity statements hold: (internal, internal-sink) permits and (internal, external-sink) escalates.

row6_sink_policy.verdict_table_status: DERIVED, not independent: every row is what the whitelist-then-severity rule above yields. It is written out because a policy whose cells cannot be read off at a glance is a policy nobody checks, and the loader asserts the rule reproduces this table exactly -- so the two can never disagree.

high_risk_actions.necessity: Externally visible and irreversible: once a message leaves, no later decision can retract it. Part I's realized_harm_F5 is defined over is_high_risk, so an empty set would leave that predicate with no positive case.

Irreversible inside the user's own store: the destructive action the frozen Omega supplies (ADR 0016 recorded that Omega supplies it without classifying it, correctly, since classification is policy and not vocabulary).

row10_oracle_classification.not_high_risk_rationale: calendar.read and notes.read are reads and change nothing; notes.write is reversible inside the user's own store. Naming them here rather than leaving the complement implicit is what makes the boundary of the set reviewable.

sensitive_labels.label: sensitive
sensitive_labels.necessity: Part I's is_sensitive selects which verified labels make an undeclassified egress a realized harm. It is the top of row 4's order, so any other choice would make the two rows disagree about which label is the dangerous one.

scope_boundary: This document freezes rows 4, 6 and 10 ONLY. It is not the task_authorization_policy (row 5, still UNSET, so F2 wrong_principal stays unscored), and it does not fix authz_context_hash, which stays ADR 0009 category (c) owned by G-15. It therefore enables the REFUSAL half of context_policy_ok and approval_artifact_ok; the ACCEPTANCE half additionally needs authz_context_hash and labelled fixtures.
